Let the wall-temperature excess be

\[
\theta_w(x)=T_w(x)-T_\infty=\theta_0 x^n,
\]

with the given condition \(n=-1\), i.e.

\[
\theta_w(x)=\frac{\theta_0}{x}.
\]

Assume a steady laminar natural-convection boundary layer on a vertical surface in a quiescent fluid, Boussinesq buoyancy, constant properties, and a finite Prandtl number. Let

\[
u=O(U),\qquad y=O(\delta),\qquad \Delta T=O(\theta_w).
\]

From the energy equation,

\[
\frac{U\theta_w}{x}\sim \alpha\frac{\theta_w}{\delta^2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
U\sim \frac{\alpha x}{\delta^2}.
\]

From the momentum equation,

\[
\frac{U^2}{x}\sim \nu\frac{U}{\delta^2}\sim g\beta\theta_w .
\]

Combining these gives the general power laws

\[
U_{\max}\sim x^{(n+1)/2},
\]

\[
\delta\sim x^{(1-n)/4},
\]

\[
q''\sim \frac{k\theta_w}{\delta}\sim x^{(5n-1)/4},
\]

\[
Q\sim x^{(5n+3)/4},
\]

\[
v(\infty)\sim \frac{U_{\max}\delta}{x}\sim x^{(n-1)/4}.
\]

For the given case \(n=-1\):

\[
\boxed{U_{\max}\sim x^0}
\]

so the maximum velocity is independent of \(x\), up to similarity-constant factors.

\[
\boxed{\delta\sim x^{1/2}}
\]

\[
\boxed{q''\sim x^{-3/2}}
\]

where \(q''\) is the local heat flux.

For the total heat transfer, the formal downstream power law is

\[
\boxed{Q\sim x^{-1/2}}.
\]

If \(Q\) is defined as the cumulative heat from a finite leading edge \(x_0\) to \(x\), then because the heat flux is singular at the leading edge, one must write, formally,

\[
Q(x)\sim x_0^{-1/2}-x^{-1/2},
\]

with a finite cutoff \(x_0\). If \(Q\) means the heat transferred downstream of \(x\), then

\[
Q(x)\sim x^{-1/2}.
\]

Finally, the edge velocity is

\[
\boxed{v(\infty)\sim x^{-1/2}}.
\]

Thus, in summary:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
u_{\max} &\sim x^0,\\
\delta &\sim x^{1/2},\\
q'' &\sim x^{-3/2},\\
Q &\sim x^{-1/2},\\
v(\infty) &\sim x^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]

The corresponding similarity variable is of the form

\[
\eta \sim \frac{y}{x^{1/2}}.
\]

Physically, the ideal condition

\[
T_w-T_\infty\propto \frac{1}{x}
\]

is singular at the exact leading edge \(x=0\): the surface temperature, local heat flux, and edge velocity all blow up as \(x\to0\), and the cumulative heat transfer from \(x=0\) is not finite. Therefore the exact mathematical solution is not physically realizable all the way to a sharp leading edge.

It can be realized physically only as a regularized or limiting flow for \(x>0\). For example, it would arise in steady laminar natural convection from a vertical surface whose surface temperature is externally maintained as

\[
T_w=T_\infty+\frac{\theta_0}{x},
\]

or equivalently whose local heat flux is distributed as

\[
q''\propto x^{-3/2},
\]

for \(x\) larger than some finite cutoff. A concrete physical approximation is a vertical surface heated by a localized source or controlled heater concentrated near the leading edge, with a finite leading-edge size or finite minimum temperature that removes the \(x=0\) singularity. It would not arise spontaneously from an ordinary isothermal or constant-heat-flux plate unless the thermal condition is tailored to produce this inverse-distance temperature distribution.
